1. INTRODUCTION
On 19 February 2025, the Commission adopted ‘A Vision for Agriculture and Food’1 setting
out a pathway for the EU actions towards achieving an attractive, competitive, resilient, future-
oriented and fair agri-food system for current and future generations of farmers and agri-food
operators. The Vision called for unnecessary bureaucratic and regulatory burden to be reduced,
a key step to support the competitiveness of the farming sector and of the entire agri-food value
chain, including a more streamlined and strategic implementation of the Common Agricultural
Policy (CAP).
On 14 May 2025, drawing on and responding to extensive feedback from stakeholders, the
Commission proposed a comprehensive simplification package of the basic legislation
underpinning the current CAP (2023-2027), that is the CAP Strategic Plan and the
Horizontal Regulations2. This package3 delivers in the following areas: (i) on-farm
simplification and streamlining of requirements to better adjust to different situations and to
various farming practices; (ii) streamlining support for smaller and medium-sized farms; (iii)
providing measures that can help boost competitiveness; and (iv) increasing Member States’
flexibility in managing CAP strategic plans (CAP Plans). With modifications, the proposal was
adopted by the co-legislators and then published on 31 December 20254.
This proposal was accompanied by a staff working document, documenting the stakeholders’
feedback and assessing impacts of the proposed changes on administrative costs borne by
farmers and national administrations5.
At the time, the Commission also published a roadmap6 to deliver additional improvements
via the CAP’s secondary legislation.
This staff working document (Section 2) provides an assessment of impacts on administrative
costs resulting from simplification of the following:
• Commission Delegated Regulation amending Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1172
concerning the integrated administration and control system (IACS) as regards the
scope of the quality assessments of the geo-spatial application system and of the area
monitoring system (changes to Articles 4 and 5 of this Delegated Regulation);
• Commission Implementing Regulation amending Implementing Regulation (EU)
2022/1173 concerning the integrated administration and CAP control system as

regards the obligation to record the use of plant protection products in the geo-spatial

and Annexes I, V and VII).
Where data for estimates was available, the impacts were quantified, otherwise the document
provides a qualitative appreciation of burden reduction7. The available figures are summarised
in the annex to this document.
This document does not cover other adjustments of the secondary legislation that solely
translate the simplifications pursued in the underlying basic act, and which were already
assessed in the above-mentioned staff working document.
2. SIMPLIFICATION MEASURES AND THEIR IMPACT ON ADMINISTRATIVE
COSTS
2.1. Amending Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1172 as regards the scope of the
quality assessments of the geo-spatial application (GSA) system and of the area
monitoring system (AMS)
The main IACS components, including GSA and AMS, are subject to an annual quality
assessment to evaluate if the IACS is achieving its aims, and to improve how it works (as
regards the correct number of hectares for the CAP´s output and result indicators)8.
The amendment introduces the following changes:
• Limiting the scope of AMS and GSA quality assessment only to monitorable
eligibility conditions, which will make it possible to simplify further the Union-level
methodology (ULM) for IACS quality assessment and considerably reduce the
necessity of field visits.
Impact on national administrations
A quantification of the impact of this change relies on the provisional information provided by
all Member States as they report their IACS quality assessments’ results in QUAP portal
(Quality Assessment Platform):
• Number of eligibility conditions for area-based interventions under the current CAP
Plans:
7 Quantification is based on many assumptions and should be viewed as such. Isolating specific administrative
costs is also difficult and limited availability of data impedes the robustness of the calculations.
8 For further information and previous improvements of this framework, see SWD(2024) 360 final of 10.12.2024
3
Overall, Member States reported 6 500 eligibility conditions. This represents an
average of 233 eligibility conditions per Member State (across 28 CAP Plans), but with
differences among them depending on the design of the interventions done by each
Member State (for instance, ten Member States have more than 300 eligibility
conditions, while eleven Member States have fewer than 150). This figure provides a
comparative insight into the design of the interventions, that can also ultimately
illustrate the greater or lesser burden of requirements that have been set.
• Rate of monitorable and non-monitorable eligibility conditions in the current design of
CAP Plans:
Overall, 54% of the reported eligibility conditions can be considered monitorable,
including administrative checks (carried out for all claimed parcels, and therefore in
line with monitoring principles applied in AMS). In contrast, 46% were reported as
non-monitorable, requiring field visits or requesting specific documentation,
performed on a sample of the population of claimed parcels. There is also a significant
variability among Member States: nine countries have more than 90% of their
eligibility conditions monitorable (four of them 100%), and three have less than 10%
of monitorable eligibility conditions. This figure is crucial, since it allows a more
accurate estimation of the intensity in the implementation of AMS.
Number of claimed parcels with at least one non-monitorable eligibility condition:
Based on the figures reported by all Member States, the number of parcels in the
samples of IACS quality assessments is around 120 000. Those which have at least one
non-monitorable eligibility condition requiring a field visit, or a similar task in terms
of workload, amount to more than 77 600 (65%). This figure of 77 600 parcels
represents the maximum workload that could be saved by public administrations.
Whenever the quality assessment sample is already part of the ‘on-the-spot checks’
sample, the workload reduction is limited. However, a certain share of the monitored
population of parcels would need field visits for the quality assessment exercise in case
the result is not conclusive (i.e. cloud cover, very small parcels). An estimation between
15-20% of field visits in monitored parcels should represent a conservative share,
according to the current capabilities of the available technology. In previous years,
between 84 000 and 86 000 parcels had field visits (77 600 + [15%/20%]*42 400),
while for claim year 2026 only 18 000 to 20 000 would need to be visited. This leads
to a final estimation of savings between 64 000 and 68 000 parcels not having to be
inspected on the field.
• Saving of costs in the IACS quality assessment exercise:
Taking the previous element into consideration, the savings could vary for each
Member State from EUR 11 000 to EUR 540 000 depending on the number of non-
monitorable eligibility conditions that are concerned. An estimation of around EUR 60
per parcel inspected (or similar task), is considered, according to the field inspections
daily gross cost of EUR 250 and an average rate of 4-5 parcels visited per day due to
the scattered location of the parcels that are part of the quality assessment samples.
4
This represents a saving of EUR 3.7-4 million (i.e. an average of EUR 3.85 million)
at EU level when this simplification enters into force for claim year 2026, which
corresponds to more than 50% of the costs of performing IACS quality assessment in
the previous years.
Impact on farmers
These changes will reduce significantly the number of on-farm visits that national authorities
need to make to perform the annual IACS quality assessment. It is currently estimated that
more than 21 000 farmers are involved in the assessment of non-monitorable eligibility
conditions every year, in the IACS quality assessment exercise, at EU level. Consequently,
these farmers will have more time to dedicate to their own work, as they will spend less time
dealing with on-farm visits by national authorities. Note that, for those interventions where the
eligibility conditions are fully monitorable, no further on-the-spot checks are needed under the
proposed system.
Overall, the proposed simplifications, combined with the full implementation of the AMS,
would reduce stress factors for farmers as a well-functioning IACS system allows farmers to
participate in CAP interventions in an efficient manner, reducing the likelihood of sanctions,
and receiving financial support in an accurate and timely manner.
The main objective of the amendment is to focus the quality assessment of the area monitoring
system and the geo-spatial application only on monitorable eligibility conditions, which are
defined in Article 10(3) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1173. This will
allow the alignment of the quality assessment exercise with the scope of the area monitoring
system. The main practical impact will be the reduction of the number of farm visits and the
burden for farmers in the context of the quality assessment exercise. However, as for the
information referring to the non-monitorable eligibility conditions, it will be based on the
results of the control systems implemented by the Member States. Therefore, the proposed
amendments do not impact the original policy objectives.
2.2. Amending Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1173 as regards the obligation to
record the use of plant protection products in the geo-spatial aid application
(GSA)
The amendment introduces the following changes:
• Deletion of the obligation that the GSA shall contain, where relevant, information
on the use of plant protection products for parcels under interventions for sustainable
and reduced use of pesticides under eco-schemes and environmental, climate-related
and other management commitments9.
Impact on national administrations
9 Articles 31 and 70 of the Regulation (EU) 2021/2115, respectively
5
The fact that the registration of plant protection products in the GSA will no longer be
mandatory will provide Member States with greater flexibility to manage their own systems,
ultimately leading to a reduction of costs since there will be no need to develop and maintain
a dedicated Information and Technologies system to manage those registries. However, these
cost reductions for national administration are not possible to quantify since it depends on the
approach taken by each Member State.
The proposed amendment does not preclude Member States from implementing that obligation
where they consider it appropriate. It should be remembered that the requirement of record-
keeping of plant protection products is necessary as laid down in the Regulation concerning
the placing of plant protection products on the market10.
Impact on farmers
The deletion of the obligation to record the use of plant protection products in the GSA is
expected to reduce the burden for farmers regarding the time spent performing this task and
allows more time to be spent on farm management or other tasks of the farmer’s choosing.
As mentioned in the Commission staff working document SWD(2025) 236, based on the
results of the simplification study, farmers spend an average of 56 hours11 annually on preparing
and submitting CAP aid applications, of which 9.6% is spent on administrative tasks related to
conditionality and 56% of that time for other elements of aid application(s) (the remainder
being recording and reporting).
Taking into consideration the above, it can be estimated that there will be a reduction by 20%12
of the overall workload for farmers for recording and reporting tasks when preparing and
submitting CAP aid applications due to the deletion of the obligation to record the use of plant
protection products, that would correspond, on average, to 4 hours per concerned GSA. In case
of use of external advisory services, due to their technical expertise, it can be estimated a
reduction on average, of 2 hours per concerned GSA.
In case of internal costs (administrative tasks performed by the beneficiary), each hour of work
is estimated to correspond to EUR 11.2513. In case of the use of external advisory services, a
sum of EUR 32.7014 per hour can be assumed as the cost incurred by a beneficiary for the tasks

CAP’ farmers taking part in the European Commission targeted consultation on simplification of 2024 declared
to spend an average of seven working days annually on administrative tasks
12 Based on expert judgment

6
related to recording and reporting plant protection products under the preparation and
submission of a GSA.
The estimated number of beneficiaries, benefitting from the deletion of the requirement to
report information on the use of plant protection products for parcels under interventions for
sustainable and reduced use of pesticides is around 3.5 million for financial year 2024 (claim
year 2023). These include beneficiaries under eco-schemes (2.8 million) and environmental,
climate-related and other management commitments (730 000). Taking these figures into
account and the fact that 78%15 of EU farmers use paid external support for aid-related
administrative tasks, this results in estimated savings up to EUR 215 million annually for
these farmers in all Member States.
The objective of the amendment is to avoid reporting the same piece of data more than once
and, therefore, does not impact the original policy objectives.
2.3. Amending Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/128 as regards the scrutiny of
transactions
Scrutiny of transactions under the CAP refers to the process of checking the validity of
transactions through financial records of beneficiaries (undertakings) as regards market
measures and sectoral interventions to ascertain whether transactions financed under the CAP
have actually been carried out and have been correctly executed. Member States need to
appoint a special service in the administration that performs this task and has the right to access
commercial documents and carry out checks in third countries as well.
The amendment entails the following:
• Simplified process for scrutiny of transactions conducted by the special service
appointed for scrutiny in the Member States.
The purpose of the change is to strike the right balance between the current relevance of
scrutiny of transactions considering the substantial evolution of the management and control
system of the CAP in the last 20 years and the resources that need to be deployed by Member
States for this specific ex-post control annually in all Member States16. The simplification
entails allowing Member States to select the sample of transactions based on a risk analysis
rather than establish a sample based on a minimum coverage.
Impacts of simplification concerning scrutiny of transactions
Currently, around 1 150 controls are carried out annually. The costs of controls may vary
depending on whether it involves checking third country undertakings on the spot or not. For
national administrations, the simplification is estimated to reduce by half the controls carried
out, but the cost savings cannot be quantified. Depending on the type of the control, this can
15 According to the aforementioned ‘Study on simplification and administrative burden for farmers and other
beneficiaries under the CAP’
16 selected on the basis of Article 46 (1)(2) and (3) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/128
7
bring benefits to CAP beneficiaries by reducing the time and cost entailed in attending a
control or providing additional information.
The proposed changes do not compromise the original policy objectives, as Member States
should have an efficient management and control system in place as per Article 59 of
Regulation (EU) 2021/2116. Furthermore, following Annex I of Regulation (EU) 2022/127
Member States should define the control system based on a risk analysis, which allows efficient
use of resources in performing the necessary controls addressing the most relevant risks. This
should in general cover the ex-spot controls as well, if considered necessary based on the risk
analysis.
Thus, in fact the proposed changes would align the requirements for scrutiny of transactions
with the general conditions set out for the overall management and control system of a Member
State.
2.4. Amending delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/126 as regards approval of
operational
programmes
of
transnational
(associations
of)
producer
organisations, market withdrawals, rules on marketing standards, and minimum
control rate for hemp cultivation
The draft amendments to this act fall into two categories:
• Amendments that solely translate simplification changes to the underlying basic acts
(CAP Strategic Plan Regulation 2021/2015 and Horizontal Regulation 2021/2016, the
“Omnibus III” proposal). These amendments do not entail any additional cost
reductions and are thus not included in this assessment. The effects of these changes
have already been assessed in a staff working document accompanying the Omnibus
III proposal17.
• Modifications that introduce additional simplification are listed and assessed in terms of
reducing administrative burden in section 2 below. Where data for estimates was
available, the impacts were quantified, otherwise the document provides a qualitative
appreciation of burden reduction18. The available figures are summarised in the annex.
The amendment introduces the following changes:
• Specification that approval of the operational programmes of transnational
(associations of) producer organisations, financed under the CAP sectoral
interventions, takes place in the Member States where these organisations have their
head offices.
• Removal of various prescriptive rules in relation to market withdrawals in sectoral
interventions managed by producer organisations implementing approved operational
17 SWD(2025) 236 final
18 Quantification is based on many assumptions and should be viewed as such. Isolating specific administrative
costs is also difficult and limited availability of data impedes the robustness of the calculations.
8
programmes (e.g. fruit and vegetable sector) financed under the sectoral CAP support
for sectors, inclusion of the transport and conditioning costs in the calculation of the
Union compensation, removal of the condition relating to the share of market
withdrawals, removal of obligations relating to documentation on the side of producers
and recipients.
• Reduction of rules on marketing standards applying to withdrawn products
• Reduction of minimum control rate for hemp cultivation supported under CAP
Plans, and more flexibility for the eligibility of hemp varieties newly registered.
Impact of simplification concerning CAP support for transnational (associations of)
Producer Organisations
Of more than 1 600 (associations of) producer organisations recognised in the EU, 45 - all in
the fruit and vegetable sector - have members located in another/other Member State. Member
State where the head offices of these transnational organisations are located are responsible for
their recognition and administrative cooperation with other Member State(s), including on
controls. The simplification clarifies responsibilities of the Member States where head offices
are located by establishing that they are also responsible for approval of the operational
programmes of these organisations.
For producer organisations, the change reduces the uncertainty as regards expenditure,
administrative management and controls of the operational programmes. By avoiding
(potential) redundancies, it results in reduced paperwork linked to potentially multiple approval
procedures in different countries and multiple controls of transnational (associations of)
producer organisations. From national administrations’ perspective, this avoids also
redundant controls carried out by several Member States.
Impact of simplification concerning CAP support when it comes to market withdrawals
In case of market disturbance situations (e.g. oversupply), recognised producer organisations
implementing operational programmes may take the decision to withdraw part of their
production from the market. There are two types of market withdrawals, for free distribution
and for other destinations (e.g. compost, industry) and the support granted to those
organisations is based on different calculation methods (e.g. depends on the market withdrawal
type, on the products, transport and conditioning costs). The Union financial assistance of 50%
of the actual expenditure incurred is increased to 100% for market withdrawals for free
distribution of fruit and vegetables provided the withdrawn volume does not exceed 5% of the
volume marketed by the producer organisation. In all other cases, the Union financial assistance
is limited to 50%. The market withdrawals in the fruit and vegetables sector amounted to
EUR 28.3 million for both free distribution and other destinations. This represents less than 1%
of the total expenditure eligible for support in this sector.
This simplification provides the following: a simplified calculation method to compensate
production costs by organisations implementing market withdrawals, and a reduction of
administrative tasks for both producer organisations and managing authorities.
9
For producer organisations, the removal of this obligation results in:
• lower administrative burden stemming from: (i) not being subject anymore to the
presentation of supporting documents, not limited to a certain type of packages, (ii) no
more requirements on the recipients, (iii) simpler marketing standards to be complied
with.
• a simplified financial support, by (i) removing the Union conditioning costs; the costs
being calculated by Member States as transport costs; (ii) including the transport and
conditioning costs in the maximum Union compensation and increasing fixing at 90%
the percentage for compensation (since conditioning costs are now including in the
amount of compensation), and (iii) removing the limit of 10% of volume withdrawn
(not foreseen in the basic act)..
For national administrations, besides eliminating administrative costs linked to maintaining
records or checking documentation, standardisation of the calculation methods for the support
will help increase the efficiency and consistency in managing the support.
Impact of simplification concerning the minimum control rate for hemp
CAP support can be granted also when farmers cultivate hemp, provided the varieties used
have a tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) content not exceeding 0.3%. Therefore, the farmers have
to use certified seeds of hemp varieties which are listed in the Common Catalogue of Varieties
of Agricultural Plant Species19. The THC content of those varieties has to be verified and should
not exceed for two consecutive years the limit of 0.3%, which is a legal requirement set in the
basic act.
The current legislation establishes a minimum, 30% control rate in relation to cultivated area
under CAP support (or 20% in case the cultivation in question received a prior authorisation).
The main aim of these controls is not to detect illegal cultivations given that the farmer declares
the areas and provides the seeds label to the control authorities, but to verify the stability of the
THC content in a given variety in different territories of the same Member State and in relation
to changing climate conditions. Notably, during COVID, the rate was reduced to 10% without
significant impacts on the correctness of the results. Moreover, from 2023 the maximum THC
limit was raised from 0.2% to 0.3%, therefore the risk of exceeding the limit is very low for
the majority of varieties which proved to be traditionally below the 0.2%. The risk remains
with the new varieties with an average THC content comprised between 0.2 and 0.3%.
The simplification entails reduction of control rate from 30% to 15% (or from 20% to 10%) of
the area declared.
Assuming, based on the trend of cultivation data, about 40 000 ha, the number of hectares to
be controlled will be reduced by 5 000 hectares (from approximately 10 000), halving not only
19https://food.ec.europa.eu/plants/plant-reproductive-material/plant-variety-catalogues-databases-information-
systems_en
10
the number of field visits and samples taken, but also the number of laboratory analyses to
determine the THC. Based on the figures of one Member State relating a ratio of on-the-spot
controls to area (one control covering 7 ha on average), and extrapolating this data to all areas
under cultivation, one arrives at 1 406 total controls. Reducing by half the number of controls
would result in the reduction of 700 controls and associated laboratory analysis, annually.
Eliminating partially the controls, leads to reduction of enforcement costs on the side of
national administrations linked to preparing on-site-visits, attending them, taking samples
and performing the analysis. Assuming that each control and analysis takes one day for two
persons involved in sampling and analysis, the cost reduction is approximately EUR 366 240
annually, using average EU values for labour costs (EUR 32.7 per hour).
For farmers, this reduces the time spent on preparing, attending and following up a single
control and half a day spent on each by a farmer, translates into an annual reduction of
administrative costs in the range of EUR 31 500 to 92 000 (700 x 4 h x 11.25 or 32.7), using
data for labour costs from the Simplification study and average EU values for labour costs.
